newsitem.title: USA: House Republicans rally to celebrate Contract.
newsitem.headline: House Republicans rally to celebrate Contract.

text.p: Republicans rallied around their "Contract with America" and embattled House Speaker Newt Gingrich Friday, holding a red, white and blue rally on the Capitol grounds.

The made-for-television, flag-bedecked celebration was held in the same spot where House Republicans in 1994 unveiled their 10-part legislative Contract and vowed to wrest control of Congress from the Democrats.
Two years later, the first Republican-led Congress in 40 years was in disarray as lawmakers squabbled with President Clinton over a funding bill to keep the government operating.

The House ethics committee Thursday also expanded the scope of a long-running investigation of charges against Gingrich, including whether he provided "reliable, accurate and complete information" to investigators.

With the presidential election less than six weeks away and Republican candidate Bob Dole still trailing President Clinton by a substantial margin in the polls, Republicans sought to parade their achievements.

Saying they had accomplished "common sense" changes for the American people, they vowed to increase their ranks in November despite what they termed vicious attacks from Democrats and unions over plans to rein in Medicare and balance the budget.

"When the Republican Congress tried to do what was right, we were answered by a demagogic ad campaign that was destructive of America, not just Republicans," Gingrich said. "But we are not frightened."
The speaker laid out a list of bills approved by the Congress including welfare reform, a free market farm law, sweeping telecommuncations law and line-item veto authority for the president.

Trying to show Republicans had cleaned up Congress, Gingrich held aloft what has become a standard Republican prop -- an ice bucket. Republicans ended twice a day ice delivery to congressional offices saving $500,000 a year.
"If there was any one symbol that I wish we could be remembered by ... it should be an ice bucket," he said.
Democratic leaders responded by focusing on two unpopular government shutdowns last year, part of a failed Republican strategy to force the White House to accept a balanced budget plan.

"You can stand on the Capitol steps and hire a brass band and blow up a lot of balloons, but you still can't make a full-scale retreat look like a full dress parade," said Senate Minority Leader Tom Daschle.
